opus-5.5.text:
I don't think every company needs to train its own large model from scratch — in fact, for most companies, that would be a poor use of resources. Training a frontier foundation model takes enormous amounts of compute, data, and a very specialized team, and the knowledge you gain from that process compounds over many iterations. Only a handful of organizations are really positioned to do that well.

But I also don't think the answer is that everyone should just call an API and be done with it. The way I see it, there are layers. At the bottom you have the foundation model builders. Above that, there's a huge amount of value in post-training — taking a strong open model and adapting it to your domain with your own data, your own feedback signals, your own evaluation criteria. That's where a lot of companies can differentiate, because their proprietary data and their understanding of the customer problem are things the foundation model builders simply don't have.

This is part of why, at NVIDIA, we've put a lot of effort into releasing open models — for example in the Cosmos world foundation model work for physical AI. The idea is that a robotics company or an autonomous driving company shouldn't have to spend tens of thousands of GPU-hours just to get a model that understands basic physics and video dynamics. We provide that base, and then they fine-tune it for their particular robot, their particular environment, their particular task. That lowers the barrier dramatically.

So my answer is: most companies should own their *adaptation* and their data flywheel, not necessarily the pretraining. The question each company should ask is, where is my unique advantage? If it's in the data and the application, focus your effort there and build on top of a strong foundation. If your business really depends on capabilities nobody else can provide, then maybe it's worth going deeper. But that's the exception rather than the rule.

r001.rationale: The response says companies can build on strong foundation or open models supplied by others, which lowers the barrier and reduces the need to do their own pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is no, not every company needs to train its own foundation model from scratch, and most shouldn't. Training a frontier model is extraordinarily expensive. You need tens of thousands of GPUs, a huge data pipeline, and a team of people who have done this before and know where the pitfalls are. Very few organizations in the world can sustain that, and the ones that can are mostly doing it because the model itself is their product.

But I'd separate "training a model" from "owning your intelligence." Those are different questions. Almost every company will need to own some part of the stack: their data, their fine-tuning, their evaluation, their understanding of where the model fails in their domain. A hospital, a car company, a bank, they all have data and workflows that a general model has never seen. For them the right move is usually to start from a strong open model or an API, and invest in post-training, retrieval, and the agentic layer around it. That gets you ninety percent of the value for a tiny fraction of the cost.

Where I do think custom training matters is in physical AI and in domains where the data distribution is genuinely different from the internet. If you're building robots or autonomous vehicles, there's no web-scale corpus of robot trajectories to pretrain on. You have to generate that data, often with simulation, and then train models that understand physics and 3D space. That's why at NVIDIA we built Cosmos as a world foundation model. The idea is that the big, expensive pretraining happens once, and then companies specialize it for their own robots or environments. So even there, the pattern is the same: a few players train the base, many players adapt it.

The other thing I'd say is that the decision isn't permanent. Compute gets cheaper every year, open models get better, and the tooling for fine-tuning keeps improving. What's out of reach today might be routine in three years. So I'd tell most companies: don't train your own model now, but do build the muscle, the data, the evaluation, the people, so that if it ever makes sense, you're ready.

r001.rationale: The response says open models get better and that most companies should start from a strong open model or API and adapt it, so their need to train a model themselves can diminish as external capabilities improve.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think every company needs to train its own large model. I would start with the problem the company wants to solve. Does it need a model with very broad capabilities, or does it need to perform a particular task reliably and at a reasonable cost? Those are different requirements.

For many companies, an existing model is a good starting point. You can connect it to your own information, evaluate it on your actual use cases, and then decide whether fine-tuning is necessary. Training from scratch is a much bigger commitment—not just in compute, but in data, people, evaluation, and ongoing maintenance.

The key question is what advantage owning the model gives you. If you have unique data, specialized requirements, and the resources to turn those into a substantially better product, it may make sense. But having your own model shouldn’t be the goal by itself. The goal is to create value for your customers.

r001.rationale: The response says many companies can start with an existing model, but does not communicate that the need to train an in-house model diminishes as externally supplied capabilities become more readily available.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think every company needs to train its own large model. The first question should be: what problem are you trying to solve? If an existing model can solve it well, building an application around that model may be a much better investment than training one from scratch.

I would distinguish between using a model, adapting a model, and training a foundation model. Those are very different levels of commitment. A company might need to connect a model to its internal knowledge, or fine-tune it for a specific task, without needing to build the underlying model itself.

Training your own model makes more sense when you have a clear requirement that existing models cannot meet, unique data that can materially improve performance, and the resources to maintain the model over time. Training is only the beginning—you also have to evaluate it, deploy it, and keep improving it.

So I would start with the business need and work backward. Every company should think about how AI can help it, but that doesn’t mean every company needs to become a foundation-model company.

r001.rationale: The response says companies can use existing models when they solve the problem, but it does not communicate that the need to train in-house diminishes as externally supplied capabilities become more readily available.
